robots.name: AgiBot A2
robots.description: AgiBot's full-size humanoid service robot, sold as the A2 and as the A2 Ultra, A2 Lite, A2 Max and A2 Pro configurations the maker's own pages name. The product page names four of the maker's own components — ActionGPT, HIMUS, VectorFlux and RTMOF — and says what each does, and the maker's open-source Link-U OS documents an end-to-end route for training a locomotion policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical A2.

robots.name: Booster T1
robots.description: Booster Robotics' small humanoid development platform, listed on its product page as "~1.2m, ~30kg, 23-41 DoFs" and sold in Basic, Standard and Customized configurations. Booster names no learned model for it; its developer guide documents Python and C++ SDKs for sending control commands, and its open-source repositories document training reinforcement-learning locomotion policies and deploying exported policies to a physical T1.

robots.name: DEEP Robotics Lite3
robots.description: DEEP Robotics' compact quadruped robot dog, sold as the Lite3 in Basic, Venture, Pro and LIDAR versions. DEEP Robotics names no learned model for it; its product page lists secondary development with a motion-control SDK, and its repositories document training a reinforcement-learning locomotion policy for the Lite3 and deploying it to the physical robot.

robots.name: Ameca
robots.description: Engineered Arts' full-size social humanoid robot with a lifelike face and a 61-degree-of-freedom body, run by the company's Tritium software suite. Engineered Arts names no learned model that drives the robot's motion; its specifications list default Tritium AI integrations with OpenAI ChatGPT, OpenAI Whisper and Amazon Poly, and its Tritium AI page says the Pro agent platform can use a range of LLMs or a custom model.

robots.name: Figure 03
robots.description: Figure AI's third-generation humanoid robot, which Figure says is designed for household tasks and built around Helix, its vision-language-action model.

robots.name: Galbot G1
robots.description: Galbot's wheeled humanoid, a dual-arm upper body with a neck, waist and leg lift on a four-wheel omnidirectional chassis, which its own page calls a "Humanoid Structural Design". Galbot's home page names the AstraBrain family of models and says what each does, its G1 page names AstraBrain as the robot's technology, and its developer platform documents an SDK with a control route for end-to-end model actions. The pages do not say which of the three models runs on which G1 configuration.

robots.name: Stretch 4
robots.description: Hello Robot's mobile manipulator, a wheeled base carrying a telescoping lift, a single arm, and a head, sold as a research and commercial platform. Its own documentation ships a grasping demo that runs two named third-party models, and its ROS 2 packages and Python bridge are published open source.

robots.name: LimX TRON 1
robots.description: LimX Dynamics' two-legged robot, which its own pages call "The First Multi-Modal Biped Robot", sold in Standard and EDU editions with a foot end that switches between point-foot, sole and wheeled modes. It has no torso or arms in its base configuration. LimX names no learned model for it; its repositories document training reinforcement-learning locomotion policies for the TRON1, deploying ONNX policies to it, and driving it from an LLM voice agent.

robots.name: NEO
robots.description: 1X's humanoid robot for the home, built to take on household chores. 1X names the models that run it, Redwood AI and the 1X World Model, and says what each does.

robots.name: Reachy Mini
robots.description: Pollen Robotics' desktop robot with a movable head, two antennas and a rotating body, sold as a kit in Wireless and Lite versions. It has no arms, legs or wheeled base. Pollen names no learned model for the robot itself; its documentation says it "is designed for AI Builders" and documents an SDK, a REST and WebSocket API, and a reference conversation app in which an LLM calls tools that move the robot.

robots.name: Spot
robots.description: Boston Dynamics' legged robot for automated sensing, inspection, and data capture. Its SDK documents a way to run your own trained model with Spot, and Boston Dynamics says it has built reinforcement learning into Spot's walking control.

robots.name: Unitree G1
robots.description: Unitree's humanoid robot, sold in a basic version and an EDU version for secondary development. Unitree names UnifoLM-VLA-0, a vision-language-action model built with G1 data, and publishes code for training a policy and deploying it to the robot.

robots.name: Unitree Go2
robots.description: Unitree's quadruped robot dog, sold in AIR, PRO, X and EDU configurations. Unitree names no learned model for it; its robotics repositories document training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical Go2 for motion control, and controlling it directly with ROS 2 messages.

robots.name: Unitree H1
robots.description: Unitree's full-size universal humanoid robot, sold as the H1 and H1-2. Unitree names no learned model for it; its robotics repositories document training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical H1 for motion control, and controlling it directly with ROS 2 messages.

robots.name: Unitree H2
robots.description: Unitree's full-size humanoid robot, sold as the H2 and the H2 EDU. Unitree names no learned model for it; its product page says a 2070 TOPS chip supports diverse intelligent models, and its reinforcement-learning repository lists the H2 among the robots it supports and registers velocity-tracking tasks for it.

robots.name: Unitree R1
robots.description: Unitree's compact humanoid robot, sold as the R1 AIR, R1, and R1 EDU, which Unitree's own site lists under its Humanoid Robot category. Unitree names no learned model for it: the product page says it integrates a large multimodal model for voice and image processing without naming one. Its product page states that the R1's joint and sensor control interfaces are fully open, and its reinforcement-learning repository registers a velocity-tracking task for the R1 and ships a deployment program for it.
